nodes.name: Gauss measure
nodes.statement: Denote by $\ga$ the Gauss measure on $\BR^n$, i.e., the probability measure with density $\gamma_0(x)=\pi^{-n/2}\, \e^{-\mod{x}^2}$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\lambda$.
differentia: density $\gamma_0(x)=\pi^{-n/2}\, \e^{-\mod{x}^2}$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure $\lambda$

nodes.name: admissible ball at scale $s$
nodes.statement: A closed Euclidean ball $B$ is called \emph{admissible} at scale $s>0$ if $$ r_B \leq s\ \min\bigl(1,1/\mod{c_B}\bigr); $$ here and in the sequel $r_B$ and $c_B$ denote the radius and the centre of $B$, respectively. We denote by $\cB_s$ the family of all balls admissible at scale $s$. For the sake of brevity, we shall refer to balls in $\cB_1$ simply as admissible balls.
nodes.statement_short: A ball is admissible at scale $s$ when its radius is at most $s\min(1,1/|c_B|)$; $\cB_s$ collects them.

nodes.name: maximal admissible ball
nodes.statement: Further, $B$ will be called \emph{maximal admissible} if $r_B = \min(1,1/\mod{c_B})$.

nodes.name: Gaussian $(1,r)$-atom
nodes.statement: Now let $r\in(1,\infty]$. A \emph{Gaussian} $(1,r)$-\emph{atom} is either the constant function $1$ or a function $a$ in $L^r(\gamma)$ supported in an admissible ball $B$ and such that \begin{equation} \int a \, \wrt \ga =0 \qquad \textnormal{and}\qquad \norm{a}{r}\leq \ga(B)^{1/r-1};\ \end{equation} here and in the whole paper, $\norm{\cdot}{r}$ denotes the norm in $L^r(\gamma)$. In the latter case, we say that the atom $a$ is associated to the ball $B $.
nodes.statement_short: An $L^r(\gamma)$ function supported in an admissible ball with vanishing Gaussian integral and normalised $L^r$ size, or the constant $1$.

nodes.name: the atomic Hardy space $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$
nodes.statement: The space $H^{1,r}(\ga)$ is then the vector space of all functions $f$ in $\lu{\ga}$ that admit a decomposition of the form $\sum_j \la_j \, a_j$ where the $a_j$ are Gaussian $(1,r)$-atoms and the sequence of complex numbers $\{\la_j\}$ is summable. The norm of $f$ in $H^{1,r}(\ga)$ is defined as the infimum of $\sum_j\mod{\la_j}$ over all representations of $f$ as above.
nodes.statement_short: Functions in $L^1(\gamma)$ admitting a summable expansion in Gaussian $(1,r)$-atoms, normed by the infimum of $\sum_j|\lambda_j|$.
nodes.genus: vector space of all functions $f$ in $\lu{\ga}$
differentia: admit a decomposition of the form $\sum_j \la_j \, a_j$ where the $a_j$ are Gaussian $(1,r)$-atoms and the sequence of complex numbers $\{\la_j\}$ is summable

nodes.name: $BMO(\gamma)$
nodes.statement: The space $BMO(\gamma)$ consists of all functions $f$ in $L^1 (\gamma)$ such that $$ \sup_{B\in\cB_1} \frac{1}{\gamma(B)}\int_B\mod{f-f_B}\wrt \gamma< \infty, $$ where $f_B$ denotes the mean value of $f$ on $B$, taken with respect to the Gauss measure. The norm of a function in $BMO(\gamma)$ is $$ \norm{f}{BMO(\gamma)}=\norm{f}{1}+\sup_{B\in\cB_1} \frac{1} {\gamma(B)}\int_B\mod{f-f_B}\wrt \gamma. $$
nodes.statement_short: Functions of bounded mean oscillation over admissible balls for the Gauss measure.

nodes.name: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator
nodes.statement: the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator $\cL=-(1/2)\Delta+x\cdot\nabla$, a natural self-adjoint Laplacian on $L^2(\gamma)$

nodes.name: grand maximal function
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \cM f(x)=\sup\set{\mod{\phi_t*f(x)}: {\phi\in \Phi},\, t>0} \end{equation} is also in $L^1(\lambda)$. Here $\Phi=\set{\phi \in C_c^1\big(B(0,1)\big): \mod{D^{\alpha}\phi}\le 1 \: \mathrm{for} \: \mod{\alpha}=0,1}$ and $\phi_t(x)=t^{-n}\phi(x/t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Supremum of $|\phi_t*f|$ over all $t>0$ and all normalised bump functions $\phi\in\Phi$.

nodes.name: local grand maximal function
nodes.statement: To characterise $H^1(\gamma)$, we introduce the \emph{local grand maximal function} defined on $L^1_{\rm loc}(\BR^n,\gamma)$ by $$ \mlo f(x)=\sup\set{\mod{\phi_t*f(x)}: {\phi\in \Phi},\: 0<t< \min(1, 1/|x|)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: The grand maximal function with dilations restricted to $0<t<\min(1,1/|x|)$, matching the admissible scale at $x$.

nodes.name: global condition $E(f)$
nodes.statement: the following additional \emph{global} condition \begin{equation} E(f)=\int_{0}^\infty x\ \left(\mod{\int_x^\infty f\wrt\gamma}+\mod{\int_{- \infty}^{-x} f\wrt \gamma}\right) \wrt\lambda(x)<\infty. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Weighted integrability of the tail masses of $f$ on $(x,\infty)$ and $(-\infty,-x)$.

nodes.name: stronger global condition $E_+(f)$
nodes.statement: the function $f$ satisfies the stronger global condition $$ E_+(f)=\int \mod{x}^2 \mod{f(x)}\wrt\gamma(x)<\infty, $$
nodes.statement_short: Finiteness of the $|x|^2$-weighted $L^1(\gamma)$ norm of $f$.

nodes.name: Lebesgue atom
nodes.statement: It deals with the classical Hardy space $H^1(\lambda)$ with respect to the Lebesgue measure and the associated standard $(1,\infty)$-atoms, called Lebesgue atoms below.
differentia: with respect to the Lebesgue measure

nodes.name: dilated ball $\rho B$
nodes.statement: Given a ball $B$ in $\BR^n$ and a positive number $\rho$, we shall denote by $\rho B$ the ball with the same centre and with radius $\rho r_B$.

nodes.name: Coincidence of $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ for $1<r<\infty$
nodes.statement: In \cite{MM} the spaces $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ were defined and proved to coincide for all $1<r<\infty$, with equivalent norms.
conclusions: the spaces $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ were defined and proved to coincide for all $1<r<\infty$, with equivalent norms

nodes.name: Scale invariance of the definitions
nodes.statement: If, in the definitions of $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$, we replace the family $\cB_1$ of admissible balls at scale $1$ by $\cB_s$ for any fixed $s>0$, we obtain the same spaces with equivalent norms, see \cite{MM}.
assumptions: we replace the family $\cB_1$ of admissible balls at scale $1$ by $\cB_s$ for any fixed $s>0$
conclusions: we obtain the same spaces with equivalent norms

nodes.name: Endpoint estimates for imaginary powers and Riesz transforms
nodes.statement: Indeed, in \cite{MM} the first two authors proved that the imaginary powers of $\cL$ are bounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$ and from $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$ and that Riesz transforms of the form $\nabla^ \alpha\cL^{-\mod{\alpha}}$ and of any order are bounded from $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$.
nodes.statement_short: Imaginary powers of $\cL$ and all-order Riesz transforms satisfy $H^1\to L^1$ and $L^\infty\to BMO$ endpoint bounds.
assumptions: Riesz transforms of the form $\nabla^ \alpha\cL^{-\mod{\alpha}}$ and of any order
conclusions: bounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$ and from $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$
bounded from $L^\infty (\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$

nodes.name: First-order Riesz transforms in dimension one
nodes.statement: In a recent paper \cite{MMS2}, the authors proved that boundedness from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$ and from $L^\infty(\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$ holds for any first-order Riesz transform in dimension one, but not always in higher dimension.
assumptions: for any first-order Riesz transform in dimension one
conclusions: boundedness from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$ and from $L^\infty(\gamma)$ to $BMO(\gamma)$ holds
but not always in higher dimension

nodes.name: Properties shared by $H^1(\gamma)$ with $H^1(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: In particular, the topological dual of $\huat{\gamma}$ is isomorphic to $BMO(\gamma)$, an inequality of John-Nirenberg type holds for functions in $BMO(\gamma)$ and the spaces $L^p(\gamma)$ are intermediate spaces between $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$ for the real and the complex interpolation methods.
nodes.statement_short: $H^1(\gamma)^*\cong BMO(\gamma)$, John-Nirenberg holds, and $L^p(\gamma)$ interpolates between them.
conclusions: the topological dual of $\huat{\gamma}$ is isomorphic to $BMO(\gamma)$
an inequality of John-Nirenberg type holds for functions in $BMO(\gamma)$
the spaces $L^p(\gamma)$ are intermediate spaces between $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$ for the real and the complex interpolation methods

nodes.name: Unboundedness of first-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Riesz transforms
nodes.statement: As shown in \cite{MMS2}, in higher dimension the first-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Riesz transforms $\partial_j\cL^{-1/2}$ are unbounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$; here $\partial_j = \partial/\partial_{x_j}$. Thus $\huat{\gamma}$ does not coincide with the space of all functions in $L^1(\gamma)$ such that $\partial_j\cL^{-1/2}f \in L^1(\gamma)$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$.
nodes.statement_short: In dimension $>1$ the Riesz-transform description fails for $H^1(\gamma)$.
conclusions: the first-order Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Riesz transforms $\partial_j\cL^{-1/2}$ are unbounded from $\huat{\gamma}$ to $L^1(\gamma)$
$\huat{\gamma}$ does not coincide with the space of all functions in $L^1(\gamma)$ such that $\partial_j\cL^{-1/2}f \in L^1(\gamma)$ for $j=1,\ldots,n$

nodes.name: Maximal characterisation of the classical Hardy space $H^1(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: We recall that the classical space $H^1(\lambda)$ can be characterised as the space of all functions $f$ in $L^1(\lambda)$ whose \emph{grand maximal function} \begin{equation} \cM f(x)=\sup\set{\mod{\phi_t*f(x)}: {\phi\in \Phi},\, t>0} \end{equation} is also in $L^1(\lambda)$. Here $\Phi=\set{\phi \in C_c^1\big(B(0,1)\big): \mod{D^{\alpha}\phi}\le 1 \: \mathrm{for} \: \mod{\alpha}=0,1}$ and $\phi_t(x)=t^{-n}\phi(x/t)$.
nodes.statement_short: Classical $H^1(\lambda)$ consists exactly of the $f\in L^1(\lambda)$ with $\cM f\in L^1(\lambda)$.
conclusions: the classical space $H^1(\lambda)$ can be characterised as the space of all functions $f$ in $L^1(\lambda)$ whose \emph{grand maximal function} \begin{equation} \cM f(x)=\sup\set{\mod{\phi_t*f(x)}: {\phi\in \Phi},\, t>0} \end{equation} is also in $L^1(\lambda)$

nodes.name: Equivalence of Gauss and Lebesgue measures on admissible balls
nodes.statement: In the following we use repeatedly the fact that on admissible balls at a fixed scale $s$, the Gauss and the Lebesgue measures are equivalent, i.e., there exists a constant $C(s)$ such that for every measurable subset $E$ of $B\in\cB_s$ \begin{equation} C(s)^{-1} \gamma(E)\le \,\gamma_0(c_B) \lambda(E)\le\,C(s)\gamma (E). \end{equation} In particular this implies that the Gauss measure is doubling on balls in $\cB_s$, with a constant that depends on $s$ (see \cite [{Prop. 2.1}]{MM}). Further, it is straightforward to see that if $B'\subset B$ are two balls and $B\in \cB_s$ then $B'$ is also in $\cB_s$.
nodes.statement_short: On $\cB_s$ balls the Gauss and Lebesgue measures are comparable, so $\gamma$ is locally doubling and admissibility passes to subballs.
conclusions: C(s)^{-1} \gamma(E)\le \,\gamma_0(c_B) \lambda(E)\le\,C(s)\gamma (E)
the Gauss measure is doubling on balls in $\cB_s$, with a constant that depends on $s$
if $B'\subset B$ are two balls and $B\in \cB_s$ then $B'$ is also in $\cB_s$

nodes.name: Equivalence of $E(f)$ and $E_+(f)$ for nonnegative $f$ in dimension one
nodes.statement: Observe that for $n=1$ and $f \ge 0$, Fubini's theorem implies that the conditions $E(f)<\infty$ and $E_+(f)<\infty$ are equivalent.
conclusions: the conditions $E(f)<\infty$ and $E_+(f)<\infty$ are equivalent

nodes.name: Atomic decomposition with atoms supported in a fixed ball
nodes.statement: If $g\in H^1(\lambda)$ and the support of $g$ is contained in a ball $B$, then $g$ has an atomic decomposition $g=\sum_k\lambda_k a_k$ where the $a_k$ are Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atoms associated to balls contained in $2B$ and \begin{equation} \sum_k \mod{\lambda_k}\le C\,\norm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: A compactly supported $H^1(\lambda)$ function decomposes into $(1,\infty)$-atoms whose balls stay inside $2B$, with controlled coefficients.
assumptions: the support of $g$ is contained in a ball $B$
conclusions: $g$ has an atomic decomposition $g=\sum_k\lambda_k a_k$ where the $a_k$ are Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atoms associated to balls contained in $2B$
\sum_k \mod{\lambda_k}\le C\,\norm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}

nodes.name: Coincidence of $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ and $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$
nodes.statement: For every $r$ in $(1,\infty)$, the spaces $H^{1,r} (\gamma)$ and $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ coincide, with equivalent norms.
conclusions: the spaces $H^{1,r} (\gamma)$ and $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ coincide, with equivalent norms

nodes.name: Support of the local grand maximal function
nodes.statement: If $f \in L^1(\ga)$ is supported in the admissible ball $B$, then $\supp \mlo f$ is contained in the ball $B' = B(c_B, R)$, where $R = 4 \min(1, 1/|c_B|).$
nodes.statement_short: $\mlo f$ stays supported in a fixed dilate of the admissible ball carrying $f$.
assumptions: $f \in L^1(\ga)$ is supported in the admissible ball $B$
conclusions: $\supp \mlo f$ is contained in the ball $B' = B(c_B, R)$, where $R = 4 \min(1, 1/|c_B|).$

nodes.name: Necessity of $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$
nodes.statement: If $f$ is in $\huat{\gamma}$, then $ \mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and \[ \norm{\mlo f}{1}\le C\norm{ f}{H^1(\ga)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Membership in $H^1(\gamma)$ forces the local grand maximal function to be integrable, with norm control.
conclusions: $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$
\norm{\mlo f}{1}\le C\norm{ f}{H^1(\ga)}

nodes.name: Maximal characterisation of $H^1(\gamma)$ in dimension one
nodes.statement: Let $n=1$, and suppose that $f$ is a function in $L^1(\gamma)$. Then $f$ is in $H^1(\gamma)$ if and only if $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E(f)<\infty$. The norms $\norm{f}{H^1(\gamma)}$ and $\norm{\mlo{f}}{L^1(\gamma)}+E(f)$ are equivalent.
nodes.statement_short: On the line, $H^1(\gamma)$ is exactly the set of $f\in L^1(\gamma)$ with $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E(f)<\infty$.
assumptions: suppose that $f$ is a function in $L^1(\gamma)$
conclusions: $f$ is in $H^1(\gamma)$ if and only if $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E(f)<\infty$
The norms $\norm{f}{H^1(\gamma)}$ and $\norm{\mlo{f}}{L^1(\gamma)}+E(f)$ are equivalent

nodes.name: Localisation of the local grand maximal function by the partition of unity
nodes.statement: For $g$ in $L^1_{\rm loc}(\gamma)$ and $x \in\BR^n$ one has \begin{equation} \mlo (g\eta_j\gamma_0)(x)\le C\ \gamma_0(c_{B_j})\ \mlo g(x)\ \1_{4 B_j} (x)\qquad \forall j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Multiplying by $\eta_j\gamma_0$ dominates the local maximal function by $\gamma_0(c_{B_j})\,\mlo g$ on $4B_j$.
conclusions: \mlo (g\eta_j\gamma_0)(x)\le C\ \gamma_0(c_{B_j})\ \mlo g(x)\ \1_{4 B_j} (x)\qquad \forall j

nodes.name: $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ belongs to $H^1(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: The function $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ is in $H^1(\lambda)$ and \begin{equation} \norm{(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0}{H^1(\lambda)}\le\,\, \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt \gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Each localised, mean-corrected piece lies in classical $H^1(\lambda)$ with norm bounded by the local mass of $\mlo f$.
conclusions: $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ is in $H^1(\lambda)$
\norm{(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0}{H^1(\lambda)}\le\,\, \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt \gamma

nodes.name: Chain estimate transporting mass to the unit ball
nodes.statement: Let $\phi _0=\gamma\big(B(0,1)\big)^{-1}\,\One_{B(0,1)}$. If $g \in L^\infty$ is supported in a maximal admissible ball $B$, then $$ \bignorm{g-\int g \wrt\gamma\,\phi _0}{H^1(\gamma)}\le C\big(1+\mod{c_B}^2\big) \gamma(B)\norm{g}{L^\infty}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Subtracting the mean against the normalised unit-ball bump costs at most $C(1+|c_B|^2)\gamma(B)\|g\|_\infty$ in $H^1(\gamma)$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$
assumptions: $g \in L^\infty$ is supported in a maximal admissible ball $B$
conclusions: \bignorm{g-\int g \wrt\gamma\,\phi _0}{H^1(\gamma)}\le C\big(1+\mod{c_B}^2\big) \gamma(B)\norm{g}{L^\infty}

nodes.name: Characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f$ is a function in $L^1(\gamma)$. If $\mlo f$ is in $L^1(\gamma)$ and \begin{equation} E_+(f)=\int \mod{x}^2 \mod{f(x)}\wrt\gamma(x) <\infty, \end{equation} then $f$ is in in $\huat{\gamma}$ and \[ \norm{f}{\huat{\gamma}} \le C \norm{\mlo f}{1} + C E_+(f). \] If $f$ is nonnegative, the conditions $\mlo{f}\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E_+(f)<\infty$ are also necessary for $f$ to be in $\huat{\gamma}$.
nodes.statement_short: In every dimension $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ plus $E_+(f)<\infty$ implies $f\in H^1(\gamma)$, and for $f\ge 0$ these conditions are also necessary.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$
assumptions: Suppose that $f$ is a function in $L^1(\gamma)$
If $\mlo f$ is in $L^1(\gamma)$ and \begin{equation} E_+(f)=\int \mod{x}^2 \mod{f(x)}\wrt\gamma(x) <\infty, \end{equation}
conclusions: then $f$ is in in $\huat{\gamma}$ and \[ \norm{f}{\huat{\gamma}} \le C \norm{\mlo f}{1} + C E_+(f). \]
the conditions $\mlo{f}\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E_+(f)<\infty$ are also necessary for $f$ to be in $\huat{\gamma}$

nodes.name: Continuous inclusions $L^p(\gamma)\subset H^1(\gamma)$ and $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$
nodes.statement: For $1<p\le\infty$, one has continuous inclusions $L^p(\gamma) \subset\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$, where $p' = p/(p-1)$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$
conclusions: one has continuous inclusions $L^p(\gamma) \subset\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$, where $p' = p/(p-1)$

nodes.name: Grand maximal function bound off $2B$
nodes.statement: We claim that the grand maximal function of $g$ satisfies \begin{equation} \cM g(x)\le\,\frac{C\,\norm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}\qquad\forall x\notin 2B. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Outside $2B$ the grand maximal function of $g$ is $O(\|g\|_1/|B|)$.
conclusions: \cM g(x)\le\,\frac{C\,\norm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}

nodes.name: $L^p(\gamma)$-boundedness of $\mlo$
nodes.statement: We claim that the operator $\mlo$ is bounded on $L^p(\gamma)$ for $1<p\le\infty$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$
conclusions: the operator $\mlo$ is bounded on $L^p(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Alternating charge example separating the two conditions
nodes.statement: For instance, let $(a_n)_1^\infty$ and $(a_n')_1^\infty$ be increasing sequences in $(2, \infty)$ such that \[ a_n + 2/a_n < a_n' \quad \mathrm{and} \quad a_n' + 2/a_n' < a_{n+1} < 2a_n \] for all $n$. Then set \begin{equation} f = \sum_1^\infty c_n \left(\frac{\chi_{(a_n,a_n+1/a_n)}}{\ga(a_n,a_n+1/a_n)} -\frac{\chi_{(a_n',a_n'+1/a_n')}}{\ga(a_n',a_n'+1/a_n')}\right) \end{equation} for some $c_n > 0$. One easily verifies that $\mlo f \in L^1(\ga)$ if and only if $\sum c_n < \infty$. But the global condition $E(f) < \infty$ is equivalent to $\sum c_n a_n(a_n' - a_n) < \infty$, which is here a stronger condition.
nodes.statement_short: A sum of far-apart $\pm$ normalised bumps for which $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ holds but $E(f)<\infty$ fails.

nodes.name: Maximal characterisation of $H^1(\gamma)$ in higher dimension
nodes.statement: We have not been able to find a similar characterisation of $\huat {\gamma}$ in higher dimension.

nodes.name: Arbitrary dimension in Section 4
nodes.statement: The dimension $n$ is now arbitrary.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Mean-value bound for the coefficients $b_j$
nodes.statement: \begin{equation} \mod{b_j} = \left|\frac{\int{f\eta_j}\wrt\gamma} {\int \eta_j \wrt \ga}\right|\le C \frac{1}{\gamma(B_j)}{\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The correction constants $b_j$ are bounded by the local $\gamma$-average of $|f|$ on $B_j$.

nodes.name: Atomic decomposition of $f$ modulo the partition-of-unity part
nodes.statement: \begin{align} f=\sum_j (f-b_j)\eta_j +\sum_j b_j \eta_j = \sum_j \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \,a_{jk} +\sum_j b_j \eta_j. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $f$ splits into a Gaussian-atom series plus the sum $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$.

nodes.name: Electrical-charge interpretation of the global condition
nodes.statement: Roughly speaking, if we interpret a function $f$ as a density of electrical charge on the real line, this global condition says that the positive and negative charges nearly balance out, so that the net charges inside the intervals $(-\infty,-x)$ and $(x,\infty)$ decay sufficiently fast as $x$ approaches $+\infty$. The condition is violated when the distance between the positive and the negative charges increases too much or the charges do not decay sufficiently fast at infinity.
nodes.statement_short: $E(f)<\infty$ says positive and negative charge nearly cancel and the tail net charges decay fast.

nodes.name: Two differences from the classical atomic Hardy space
nodes.statement: The definition of the space $\huat{\ga}$ closely resembles the atomic definition of the classical Hardy space $H^1(\lambda)$ on $\BR^n$ endowed with the Lebesgue measure $\lambda$, but there are two basic differences. First, the measured metric space $(\BR^n, d, \ga) $ is non-doubling. Further, except for the constant atom, a Gaussian atoms must have ``small support'', i.e., support contained in an admissible ball. Despite these differences, $H^1(\gamma)$ shares many of the properties of $H^1(\lambda)$.
nodes.statement_short: The Gaussian setting is non-doubling and its atoms must have small support, yet $H^1(\gamma)$ behaves much like $H^1(\lambda)$.

nodes.name: Three classical definitions of $H^1(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: It is well known that the classical Hardy space $H^1(\lambda)$ can be defined in at least three different ways: the \emph {atomic} definition, the \emph{maximal} definition and the definition based on \emph{Riesz transforms} \cite{CW, St2}.

nodes.name: $H^1$-$BMO$ theory on general measured metric spaces
nodes.statement: We remark that a similar $H^1-BMO$ theory for more general measured metric spaces has been developed by A. Carbonaro and the first two authors in \cite{CMM1, CMM2, CMM3}.

nodes.name: Convention on the constant $C$
nodes.statement: In the following $C$ denotes a constant whose value may change from occurrence to occurrence and which depends only on the dimension $n$, except when otherwise explicitly stated.

nodes.name: Status of the auxiliary decomposition lemma in the literature
nodes.statement: The result is probably well known, but we include a proof because we have not been able to find a reference in the literature. Some related results can be found in \cite{CKS} and \cite{CMS}.

nodes.name: Proof of the atomic decomposition lemma
nodes.statement:
In this proof, all atoms are Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atoms. We claim that the grand maximal function of $g$ satisfies  egin{equation} \cM g(x)\le\, rac{C\,
orm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}\qquad orall x
otin 2B. \end{equation} To prove this, take $x 
otin 2B$ and observe that $$ \cM g(x) =\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\, \sup_{t\ge d(x,B)}\mod{\phi_t*g(x)}, $$ since $\phi_t*g(x)=0$ for $0<t < d(x,B)$. Because of the vanishing integral of $g$, one has for $\phi\in \Phi$ and $t \ge d(x,B)$  egin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*g(x)}&\le \,\int_{B}\mod{\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_B)}\,\mod{g (y)} \wrt\lambda(y) \ & \le\,C\,t^{-n-1}\int_{B}\mod{y-c_{B}}\,\mod{g(y)}\wrt\lambda(y)\ &\le\,  rac{C\,r_{B}}{d(x,B)^{n+1}}\, 
orm{g}{1}\ &\le\,  rac{C }{\mod{B}}\, 
orm{g}{1}. \end{align*} \par For each integer $k$, denote by $\Omega_k$ the level set $\set{x: \cM g(x)>2^k}$. Then (ef{MgIc}) implies that  egin{equation} \Omega_k\subset 2B \quad 	extrm{when}\quad 2^k \ge  rac{C\, 
orm{g}{1}\,}{ \mod{B}}. \end{equation} Let $\Omega_k= igcup_i Q^k_i$ be a Whitney decomposition of $ \Omega_k$ into closed cubes $Q^k_i, \; i \in \BN$, whose interiors are disjoint, and whose diameters are comparable to $\delta$ times their distances from $\Omega_k^c$, where $\delta$ is a (small) positive constant to be chosen later. Define $	ilde{Q}_i^k$ as the cube with the same centre as $Q_i^k$ and side length expanded by a factor $2$. Then $ igcup_i	ilde{Q}^k_i= \Omega_k$ and the family $\set{	ilde{Q}^k_i: i\in \BN}$ will have the bounded overlap property, uniformly in $k$, provided that $\delta$ is small enough. Proceeding as in the proof of the atomic decomposition for $H^1(\lambda)$ in \cite[p. 107--109]{St2}, one shows that there exists a decomposition  egin{equation} g=\sum_{k,i} A^k_i, \end{equation} with the following properties.  egin{itemize} \item[mi] Each function $A^k_i$ is supported in a ball $B^k_i$ that contains the cube $	ilde{Q}^k_i$ as well as those $	ilde{Q}^{k+1}_m$ that intersect $	ilde{Q}^k_i$. Moreover, if $\delta$ is sufficiently small, the ball $B^k_i$ is contained in $\Omega_k$ and for each $k$ the family $\set{B^k_i}_i$ has the bounded overlap property. \item[] \item[mii] $A^k_i=\lambda_{k,i} \,a^k_i$, where $a^k_i$ is a Lebesgue atom associated to the ball $B^k_i$ and $$\sum_{k,i} \mod{\lambda_{k,i}}\le C\, 
orm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. $$ \item[] \item[miii] $\mod{A^k_i}\le C\,2^k$ for each $k$ and $i$. \end{itemize} We split the sum in (ef{ad}) in two parts  egin{align*} g&=\sum_{B^k_i
ot\subset 2B}A^k_i\ +\sum_{B^k_i\subset 2B} A^k_i =\Sigma_1+\Sigma_2. \end{align*} Clearly, $\Sigma_2$ is an atomic decomposition with atoms associated to balls contained in $2B$. Thus, it suffices to show that $ \Sigma_1$ is a multiple of an atom associated to $2B$. And indeed, $\Sigma_1$ is supported in $2B $ and has integral zero, because it is the difference of $g$ and $ \Sigma_2$, both of which have these two properties. Moreover, by mi\ and miii\ $$ \mod{\sum_i A^k_i}\le C\,2^k. $$ Hence by (ef{hi}) $$ \mod{\Sigma_1}\le\sum_{ 2^k \,<\,C\,
orm{g}{1}/\mod{B}}\mod {\sum_i A^k_i}\le  rac{C\,
orm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}\le  rac{C}{\mod {2B}}\,
orm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. $$ Thus $\Sigma_1$ is a multiple of an atom associated to $2B$. We thus have the desired atomic decomposition of $g$, and the norm estimate (ef{ne}) also follows.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\cM g$ off $2B$, run a Whitney/level-set atomic decomposition of $g$, then absorb the atoms whose balls leave $2B$ into a single multiple of an atom on $2B$.

nodes.name: Proof of the coincidence of $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ and $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$
nodes.statement_short: Transfer a Gaussian $(1,r)$-atom to a Lebesgue atom via $\gamma_0$, apply Lemma \ref{cptsupp} to split it into $(1,\infty)$-Lebesgue atoms in $2B$, and pull back to Gaussian $(1,\infty)$-atoms.

nodes.name: Proof of the support lemma
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \supp \mlo f$. We write $\rho = |x|$ and $c = |c_B|,$ so that $B \subset B(c_B, \min(1,1/c))$. The balls $B$ and $B(x, \min(1,1/\rho))$ must intersect, and so \begin{equation} |x-c_B| \le \min(1,1/c) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation} To prove the lemma, it is enough to show that \begin{equation} \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3 \min(1,1/c), \end{equation} since it then follows that $x \in B'$. Now $c - \rho \le |x-c_B|$, so that (\ref{eq:dist}) implies \[ c - \min(1,1/c) \le \rho + \min(1,1/\rho). \] Considering the cases $c \le 1$ and $c > 1$, we conclude from this that \begin{equation} \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation} The function $t \mapsto t^{-1} - t, \;\; t>0$, and its inverse are clearly decreasing. Considering the values of this function at $t = \min(1,1/c)$ and $\min(1,1/\rho)/3$, we see that (\ref{eq:3}) is equivalent to \[ \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho). \] Because of (\ref{eq:le}), this inequality follows if \[ \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho) \] or equivalently $\frac43 \min(1,1/\rho) \le 2\max(1,\rho),$ which is trivially true. We have proved (\ref{eq:3}) and the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the scale comparison $\min(1,1/\rho)\le 3\min(1,1/c)$ and verify it by case analysis on $c$ plus monotonicity of $t\mapsto t^{-1}-t$.

nodes.name: Proof of the necessity of $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$
nodes.statement: We shall prove that for any Gaussian atom $a$ \begin{equation} \norm{\mlo a}{1}\le C, \end{equation} from which the lemma follows. \par Since (\ref{MaEa}) is obvious if $a$ is the constant function $1$, we assume that $a$ is associated to an admissible ball $B$. By the preceding lemma, $\supp \mlo f$ is contained in the ball denoted $B'$. \par The integral of $\mlo a$ over $2B$ with respect to $\ga$ is no larger than $C$, since $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a \le C \sup |a| \le C/\gamma(B)$. To estimate $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a$ at a point $x$ in the remaining set $B'\setminus 2B$, we take $\phi \in \Phi$ and $0 < t < \min(1,1/\mod{x})$ and estimate $a*\phi_t(x)$. We can assume that $t > d(x, B)$ so that $t > |x-c_B|/2$, since otherwise $\phi_t*a(x)$ will vanish. Write \begin{equation} \phi_t*a(x) = t^{-n} \int \left(\phi\big(\frac{x-y}t\big) -\phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big)\right)\,a(y) \wrt y + t^{-n} \phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big) \int a(y) \wrt y. \end{equation} Here the first term to the right can be estimated in a standard way by $$ C t^{-n-1} \int_B |y-c_B| \, |a(y)| \wrt y \le C\ |x-c_B|^{-n-1}\ r_B\ \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}. $$ To deal with the second term, we estimate $\int a(y)\wrt y$, knowing that the integral of $a$ against $\ga$ vanishes. Thus $$ \int a(y)\wrt y = \int a(y) \frac{\ga_0(c_B) - \ga_0(y)}{\ga_0(c_B)}\wrt y. $$ The fraction appearing here is \begin{equation} e^{|c_B|^2}\left(e^{-|c_B|^2} - e^{-|y|^2}\right) = 1 - e^{(c_B-y)\cdot(c_B+y)}, \end{equation} and the last exponent stays bounded for $y \in B$. Thus the modulus of the right-hand side of (\ref{eq:fraction}) is at most $C|c_B-y| |c_B+y| \le C r_B (1+|c_B|).$ Since $\int |a|\,d\ga \le 1$, this implies \[ |\int a(y)\wrt y| \le C r_B (1+|c_B|) \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}. \] For the last term in (\ref{eq:max}), we thus get the bound $C |x-c_B|^{-n} r_B (1+|c_B|) \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}$. Putting things together, we conclude that for $x \in B'\setminus 2B$ $$ \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a(x) \le C |x-c_B|^{-n-1} r_B \ga_0(c_B)^{-1} + C |x-c_B|^{-n} r_B (1+|c_B|) \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}. $$ An integration with respect to $\wrt \ga$, or equivalently $\ga_0 \wrt \lambda$, then leads to $$ \int_{B'\setminus 2B} \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a(x)\wrt \ga(x) \le C + C r_B (1+|c_B|) \log\frac{\min(1,1/|c_B|)}{r_B} \le C, $$ and (\ref{MaEa}) is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to a single atom, bound $\mlo a$ trivially on $2B$ and by a standard cancellation/Taylor estimate on $B'\setminus 2B$, then integrate.

nodes.statement:
Since the support of $\eta_j$ is contained in $B_j$, the support of $\mlo (g\eta_j\gamma_0)$ is contained in the ball $4B_j$, because of Lemma ef{supp}. Moreover, for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $x \in 4B_j$ $$ \phi_t*(g\eta_j\gamma_0)(x)=\gamma_0(c_{B_j})\ 	ilde{\phi}_t*g(x), $$ where $	ilde{\phi}(z)=\phi(z)\eta_j(x-tz)\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_ {B_j})$. Thus, to prove (ef{2maxf}) it suffices to show that there exists a constant $C$ such that $	ilde{\phi}\in C\Phi$ for $x\in 4B_j$ and $0<t < \min(1, 1/\mod{x})$. The support of $	ilde{\phi}$ is contained in $B(0,1)$ and $$ \mod{	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le  rac{\gamma_0(x-tz)}{\gamma_0(c_{B_j})}\le C, $$ because for $|z| \le 1$  egin{align*} \mod{x-tz-c_{B_j}}\le \mod{x-c_{B_j}}+\mod{tz} \le C\,{\min(1, 1/\mod{c_{B_j}})}. \end{align*} Similarly $\mod{
abla	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le C$, because the gradients $

nodes.name: Proof that $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\in H^1(\lambda)$
nodes.statement: By the maximal characterisation of the classical space $H^1(\lambda) $, it suffices to show that \begin{equation} \int\cM\left( (f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\right)\wrt\lambda(x)\le \,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma. \end{equation} Because of (\ref{3d}), all that needs to be verified is that \begin{equation} \int\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\ \sup_{t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})} \mod{((f-b_j) \eta_j\gamma_0\big)*\phi_t(x)}\wrt\lambda(x) \le \,C\, \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt \gamma. \end{equation} To prove (\ref{6th}), we split the integral in the left-hand side into the sum $$ \int_{4B_j}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x)+\int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x). $$ If $x\in 4B_j$, then for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})$ \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le t^{-n} \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)-b_j}\wrt \gamma(y)\\ &\le (1+\mod{x})^n\int _{B_j}\big(\mod{f(y)}+\mod{b_j}\big)\wrt\gamma (y) \\ \qquad&\le C\,(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n\ \,\int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\wrt\gamma(y), \end{align*} the last inequality because of (\ref{1st}). Hence \begin{align*} \int_{4B_j} \cdots \wrt\lambda(x)\, \le \,C\, \ \mod {4B_j}\ (1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n \int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma \, \le\, C\,\int_{B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma . \end{align*} If $x\in (4B_j)^c$, we take $\phi$ and $t$ as before and observe that we can assume that $t> d(x, B_j)$, since otherwise the convolution in (\ref{6th}) will vanish. In view of (\ref{mz}) and (\ref{1st}), we then get \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le\int _{B_j}\mod {\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_{B_j})}\ \mod{ f(y)-b_j}\,\eta_j(y) \wrt \gamma(y) \\ &\le\,C\, t^{-n-1} \int_{B_j} \mod{y-c_{B_j}}\,\mod{f(y)-b_j}\wrt \gamma (y)\\ &\le \,C\,\frac{1}{d(x,B_j)^{n+1}} r_{B_j}\, \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\wrt\gamma(y). \end{align*} This implies that $$ \int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x)\le C\,\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma\le C\, \int_{B_j} \mlo f \wrt \gamma. $$ We have proved (\ref{6th}) and the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: By the classical maximal characterisation, reduce to the large-$t$ part of $\cM$ and estimate it separately on $4B_j$ and on its complement.

nodes.name: Proof of the maximal characterisation in dimension one
nodes.statement:
Suppose that $f\in\huat{\gamma}$. Then $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ by Lemma ef{necn}. To prove the necessity of the condition $E(f)<\infty$, it suffices to show that $E(a)<C$ for all Gaussian atoms $a$. This is obvious for the exceptional atom $1$. If $a$ is associated to a ball $B \in \cB_1$, it follows from the inequality $$ \mod{\int_{-\infty}^{-x} a\wrt\gamma}+\mod{\int_{x}^{\infty} a\wrt \gamma}\le \ \1_B(x). $$ Conversely, assume that $f$ is a function in $L^1(\gamma)$ such that $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E(f)<\infty$. We shall prove that $f\in H^1(\gamma)$, by constructing a Gaussian atomic decomposition $f= \sum_j\lambda_j\,a_j$ such that $\sum_j \mod{\lambda_j}\le C  ig (
orm{\mlo f}{1}+E(f) ig)$. \par Most of the following argument, up to the decomposition (ef{aat}), works also in the $n$-dimensional setting. Since we shall need it in the next section, we carry out that part in $\BR^n$.\par By subtracting a multiple of the exceptional atom $1$, we may without loss of generality assume that  egin{equation} \int f\wrt\gamma=0. \end{equation} Let $\set{B_j}$ be a covering of $\BR^n$ by maximal admissible balls. We can choose this covering in such way that the family $\set{ rac12 B_j}$ is disjoint and $\set{4 B_j}$ has bounded overlap \cite[Lemma 2.4]{GMST1}. Moreover, for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $x \in 4B_j$ $$ \phi_t*(g\eta_j\gamma_0)(x)=\gamma_0(c_{B_j})\ 	ilde{\phi}_t*g(x), $$ where $	ilde{\phi}(z)=\phi(z)\eta_j(x-tz)\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_ {B_j})$. Thus, to prove (ef{2maxf}) it suffices to show that there exists a constant $C$ such that $	ilde{\phi}\in C\Phi$ for $x\in 4B_j$ and $0<t < \min(1, 1/\mod{x})$. The support of $	ilde{\phi}$ is contained in $B(0,1)$ and $$ \mod{	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le  rac{\gamma_0(x-tz)}{\gamma_0(c_{B_j})}\le C, $$ because for $|z| \le 1$  egin{align*} \mod{x-tz-c_{B_j}}\le \mod{x-c_{B_j}}+\mod{tz} \le C\,{\min(1, 1/\mod{c_{B_j}})}. \end{align*} Similarly $\mod{
abla	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le C$, because the gradients $ 
abla_z\eta_j (x-tz)$ and $
abla_z\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_{B_j})$ give the factors $t(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})$ and $t\mod{x-tz}\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_{B_j})$, respectively, both of which are bounded. This concludes the proof of Lemma ef{Lemma1}. \end{proof} Continuing the proof of Theorem ef{char}, we define $b_j\in\BC$ for each $j \in \BN$ by  egin{equation} \int_{-\infty}^\infty (f-b_j)\eta_j \wrt \gamma =0. \end{equation} Note that since $\eta_j=1$ on $ rac12 B_j$,  egin{equation} \mod{b_j} = \left| rac{\int{f\eta_j}\wrt\gamma} {\int \eta_j \wrt \ga}ight|\le C  rac{1}{\gamma(B_j)}{\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma}. \end{equation} We now apply Lemma ef{Lemma1} with $g=f - b_j$ and use the subadditivity of $\mlo$ combined with (ef{1st}), to get  egin{align} \int \mlo ig((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0 ig)\wrt\lambda&\le\,C\, \int_{4B_j} \mlo f \, \gamma_0(c_{B_j})\wrt\lambda \,+\,C\,  rac {\ga(4B_j)}{\ga(B_j)}\int_{B_j} \mod{f}\wrt \gamma 
onumber \ &\le\,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma. \end{align} \par  egin{lemma} The function $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ is in $H^1(\lambda)$ and  egin{equation} 
orm{(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0}{H^1(\lambda)}\le\,\, \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt \gamma. \end{equation} \end{lemma}  egin{proof} By the maximal characterisation of the classical space $H^1(\lambda) $, it suffices to show that  egin{equation} \int\cM\left( (f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0ight)\wrt\lambda(x)\le \,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma. \end{equation} Because of (ef{3d}), all that needs to be verified is that  egin{equation} \int\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\ \sup_{t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})} \mod{((f-b_j) \eta_j\gamma_0 ig)*\phi_t(x)}\wrt\lambda(x) \le \,C\, \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt \gamma. \end{equation} To prove (ef{6th}), we split the integral in the left-hand side into the sum $$ \int_{4B_j}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x)+\int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x). $$ If $x\in 4B_j$, then for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})$  egin{align*} \mod{\phi_t* ig((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0 ig)(x)}&\le t^{-n} \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)-b_j}\wrt \gamma(y)\ &\le (1+\mod{x})^n\int _{B_j} ig(\mod{f(y)}+\mod{b_j} ig)\wrt\gamma (y) \ \qquad&\le C\,(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n\ \,\int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\wrt\gamma(y), \end{align*} the last inequality because of (ef{1st}). Hence  egin{align*} \int_{4B_j} \cdots \wrt\lambda(x)\, \le \,C\, \ \mod {4B_j}\ (1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n \int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma \, \le\, C\,\int_{B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma . \end{align*} If $x\in (4B_j)^c$, we take $\phi$ and $t$ as before and observe that we can assume that $t> d(x, B_j)$, since otherwise the convolution in (ef{6th}) will vanish. In view of (ef{mz}) and (ef{1st}), we then get  egin{align*} \mod{\phi_t* ig((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0 ig)(x)}&\le\int _{B_j}\mod {\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_{B_j})}\ \mod{ f(y)-b_j}\,\eta_j(y) \wrt \gamma(y) \ &\le\,C\, t^{-n-1} \int_{B_j} \mod{y-c_{B_j}}\,\mod{f(y)-b_j}\wrt \gamma (y)\ &\le \,C\, rac{1}{d(x,B_j)^{n+1}} r_{B_j}\, \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\wrt\gamma(y). \end{align*} This implies that $$ \int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x)\le C\,\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma\le C\, \int_{B_j} \mlo f \wrt \gamma. $$ We have proved (ef{6th}) and the lemma. \end{proof} We can now finish the proof of Theorem ef{char}. By Lemmata ef{Lemma2} and ef{cptsupp}, each function $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ has an atomic decomposition $ \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \alpha_{jk}$ where the $\alpha_{jk}$ are Lebesgue atoms with supports in $2B_j$ and $$ \sum_k \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le \,C\, \int_{4B_j} \mlo f \wrt\gamma. $$ As we saw in the proof of Theorem ef{1infty}, each $a_{jk}=\gamma_0^{-1} \alpha_{jk}$ is a multiple of a Gaussian atom, with a factor which is independent of $j$ and $k$. Thus  egin{align} f=\sum_j (f-b_j)\eta_j +\sum_j b_j \eta_j = \sum_j \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \,a_{jk} +\sum_j b_j \eta_j. \end{align} and $$ \sum_{j,k} \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le \sum_j \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma \le \,C\, 
orm{\mlo f}{L^1(\gamma)}. $$ To complete the proof of Theorem ef{char}, we need to find an atomic decomposition of $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$. It is here that we must restrict ourselves to the one-dimensional case and that the global condition $E(f) <\infty$ plays a role. \par Choose the intervals $I_0=(-1,1)$, $I_j=(\sqrt{j-1}, \sqrt{j+1})$ for $j\ge 1$ and $I_j=-I_{\mod{j}}$ for $j\le -1$. The intervals $I_j$ have essentially the same properties as the balls $B_j$ introduced above, and we can use them instead of the $B_j$ to construct $\eta_j$ and $b_j$ as before. To decompose now $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$, we first normalise the functions $\eta_j$, letting \[ 	ilde{\eta}_j =  rac{\eta_j}{\int \eta_j \wrt \ga}. \] Then $b_j\eta_j = \int f \eta_j \wrt \ga \; 	ilde{\eta}_j$, and clearly \[ \sum_{j\ge k}\int f \eta_j \wrt \ga = \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga, \quad k \in \BZ, \] where $\mu_k(x) = \sum_{j\ge k} \eta_j(x).$ Notice that $\int f \mu_k \wrt \ga 	o 0$ as $k 	o \pm \infty$, in view of (ef{int0}). A summation by parts now yields  egin{equation} \sum_{j\in \BZ} \int f \eta_j \wrt \ga \; 	ilde{\eta}_j = \sum_{k\in \BZ} \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga \; (	ilde{\eta}_k - 	ilde{\eta}_{k-1}). \end{equation} But $	ilde{\eta}_k - 	ilde{\eta}_{k-1}$ is $C$ times a Gaussian atom, if we use admissible balls at some scale $s>1$ in the definition of atoms. Thus (ef{eq:**}) is our desired atomic decomposition of $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$, provided we can estimate the coefficients by showing that  egin{equation} \sum_{k\in \BZ}\left| \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga ight| \le\,C\,\left(
orm{f}{1}+ E(f)ight). \end{equation} To this end, observe that $$ \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga =\int f(x)\int_{-\infty}^x\mu'_k(y)\wrt\lambda(y)\wrt\gamma(x)=\int \mu'_k(y)\int_y^\infty f(x)\wrt\gamma(x)\wrt\lambda(y). $$ Since the support of $\mu'_k$ is contained in $I_k$ and $$ \mod{\mu_k'(y)}\,\le\,  rac{C}{\mod{I_k}}\,\le\, C \, ig(1+\mod{c_{I_k}}  ig), $$ we obtain, using also the bounded overlap of the $I_j$,  egin{align*} \sum_{k\in \BZ}\left| \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga ight| &\,\le\,C \sum_k\int_{I_k} ig(1+\mod{c_{I_k}} ig)\ \mod{\int_y^\infty f(x)\wrt\gamma(x)}\wrt\lambda(y) \ &\le C\int_{-\infty}^\infty (1+\mod{y}) \mod{\int_y^\infty f\wrt \ga}\wrt \lambda(y) \ &= C\int_{0}^\infty (1+y) \left(\mod{\int_y^\infty f\wrt \ga}+\mod{\int_{-y} ^\infty f\wrt \ga}ight)\wrt\lambda(y) \ &\le\, C ig(
orm{f}{1}+ \,E(f) ig); \end{align*} here we used (ef{int0}). This concludes the proof of Theorem ef{char}.
nodes.statement_short: Necessity from Lemma \ref{necn} and an atomwise bound; conversely, localise $f$ by a partition of unity over maximal admissible balls, atomise each piece via $H^1(\lambda)$, and in dimension one decompose $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$ by summation by parts controlled by $E(f)$.

nodes.name: Proof of the chain lemma
nodes.statement:
We shall construct atoms whose supports form a chain connecting $B(0,1)$ to $B$. First we define a finite sequence of maximal admissible balls \[ 	ilde{B} _0 = B(0,1),\, 	ilde{B}_1, \ldots, 	ilde{B}_{N }, \] all with centres $c_{	ilde{B}_{j}}$ on the segment $[0, c_B]$. The absolute values $ho_j= |c_{	ilde{B}_{j}}|$ shall be increasing in $j$, and the boundary $\partial 	ilde{B}_j$ shall contain $c_{	ilde{B}_{j-1}}$ for $j = 1,\ldots,N-1$, which means that  egin{align} ho_{j} -  rac{1}{ho_{j}}=ho_{j-1}, \qquad j=1, \ldots,N-1, \end{align} and $ho_{0} = 0, \; \;ho_{1} = 1$. Finally, $N$ is defined so that $	ilde{B}_{N-1}$ is the first ball of the sequence that contains $c_B$, and $	ilde{B}_{N } = B.$ Squaring (ef{recursive}), we get $$ ho_{j}^2-ho_{j-1}^2=2 -  rac1{ho_{j}^2}\ge1, $$ so that $ho_{N-1}^2 \ge N-1$. It follows that  egin{equation} N \le |c_B|^2 + 1. \end{equation} \par Next, we denote by $B _j, \;\;j=1,\ldots, N$, the largest ball contained in $	ilde{B}_j \cap	ilde{B}_{j-1} $. Notice that the three balls $	ilde{B}_j, 	ilde{B}_{j-1}$ and $B _j$ have comparable radii and comparable Gaussian measures. Define now functions $\phi _j$ and $g _j$ by setting  egin{align*} \phi _j&=\gamma(B _j )^{-1} \One_{B _j } \quad j=1,\ldots,N, \ g _j &= \int g \wrt\gamma\, \left(\phi_{j} -\phi _{j-1} ight), \quad j=1,\ldots,N, \ g_{N+1} &=g -\int g \wrt \gamma \: \phi_{N}. \end{align*} Clearly,  egin{equation} g-\int g\wrt\gamma\: \phi_0 = \sum_{j=1}^{N+1} g _j. \end{equation} Each function $g _j$ is a multiple of an atom. Indeed, its integral against $\gamma$ vanishes. Moreover, if $1 \le j \le N$, the support of $g _j$ is contained in $	ilde{B} _{j-1}$ and  egin{align*} 
orm{g _j}{\infty}\le (\gamma(B_{j})^{-1} + \gamma(B_{j-1})^{-1}) \int \mod{g}\wrt\gamma\, \le \,C\, \gamma(	ilde{B}_{j-1})^{-1}\ \gamma (B)\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} The support of $\phi_{N+1}$ is contained in $B$ and  egin{align*} 
orm{g_{N+1}}{\infty}\le 
orm{g}{\infty}+\gamma(B)^ {-1}\int \mod{g}\wrt\gamma \le\,C\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} Thus $$ 
orm{g _j}{H^1(\gamma)}\le C\,\gamma(B)\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,N+1. $$ Summing the coefficients in the atomic decomposition (ef{sumgj}), we then obtain via (ef{balls})  egin{align*} 
orm{g-\int g\wrt\gamma\,\phi_0}{\huat{\gamma}} \,\le\, C\, (N+1) \,\gamma(B) 
orm{g}{L^\infty} \, \le\,C (1+\mod{c_B}^2)\,\gamma(B) \,
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} The proof of the lemma is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Build a chain of $N\le |c_B|^2+1$ maximal admissible balls from $B(0,1)$ to $B$, write the difference as a telescoping sum of atoms, and add up the coefficients.

nodes.name: Proof of the characterisation of nonnegative functions
nodes.statement_short: Reuse the partition-of-unity decomposition from Theorem \ref{char}, control $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$ with the chain Lemma \ref{trch} and $E_+(f)$; necessity follows from $|x|^2\in BMO(\gamma)$ and $H^1$-$BMO$ duality.

nodes.name: Proof of the inclusions $L^p(\gamma)\subset H^1(\gamma)$ and $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$
nodes.statement:
We claim that the operator $\mlo$ is bounded on $L^p(\gamma)$ for $1<p\le\infty$. Deferring momentarily the proof of this claim, we complete the proof of the corollary. Suppose that $f$ is in $L^p (\gamma)$. Then $\mlo f$ is in $L^1(\gamma)$, because $$ 
orm{\mlo f}{1}\le 
orm{\mlo f}{p}\, \le C 
orm{f}{p}<\infty, $$ since $\gamma(\BR^n)=1$. Moreover, $E_+(f)\le 
orm{\mod{x}^2}{p'}\, 
orm{f}{p} < \infty$, by H"older's inequality. Thus $f\in \huat{\gamma}$ by Theorem ef{pos}. It also follows that the inclusion $L^p(\gamma)\subset \huat{\gamma}$ is continuous, and by duality we get the continuous inclusion $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$.\par It remains to prove the claim. We shall use again the covering $\{B_j\}$ from the proof of Theorem ef{char}. First we observe that the inequality  egin{equation} 
orm{\mlo g}{p} \le C
orm{g}{p} \end{equation} holds when $\supp g \subset B_j$, with a constant $C$ independent of $j$. Indeed, $\mlo$ is bounded on $L^p(\la)$, and $\mlo g$ is supported in the ball $4B_j$, where the Gaussian measure is essentially proportional to $d\la$. Given a function $f \in L^p(\ga)$, we write it as a sum $f = \sum f_j$ with $\supp f_j \subset B_j$ and with the sets $\{f_j 
e 0\}$ pairwise disjoint. We can then apply (ef{eq:Lp}) to each $f_j$ and sum.
nodes.statement_short: From $L^p$-boundedness of $\mlo$ and Holder's bound on $E_+(f)$, apply Theorem \ref{pos}; the $BMO$ inclusion follows by duality, and the claim from the local $L^p$ bound summed over the covering.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Claim the off-$2B$ bound for $\cM g$
nodes.statement: In this proof, all atoms are Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atoms. We claim that the grand maximal function of $g$ satisfies \begin{equation} \cM g(x)\le\,\frac{C\,\norm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}\qquad\forall x\notin 2B. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: State the pointwise bound $\cM g\lesssim \|g\|_1/|B|$ outside $2B$.

nodes.name: Prove the bound using cancellation of $g$
nodes.statement:
To prove this, take $x 
otin 2B$ and observe that $$ \cM g(x) =\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\, \sup_{t\ge d(x,B)}\mod{\phi_t*g(x)}, $$ since $\phi_t*g(x)=0$ for $0<t < d(x,B)$. Because of the vanishing integral of $g$, one has for $\phi\in \Phi$ and $t \ge d(x,B)$  egin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*g(x)}&\le \,\int_{B}\mod{\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_B)}\,\mod{g (y)} \wrt\lambda(y) \ & \le\,C\,t^{-n-1}\int_{B}\mod{y-c_{B}}\,\mod{g(y)}\wrt\lambda(y)\ &\le\,  rac{C\,r_{B}}{d(x,B)^{n+1}}\, 
orm{g}{1}\ &\le\,  rac{C }{\mod{B}}\, 
orm{g}{1}. \end{align*} \par
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $t\ge d(x,B)$ and use the vanishing integral of $g$ with a first-order Taylor estimate.

nodes.name: Whitney decomposition of the level sets
nodes.statement: For each integer $k$, denote by $\Omega_k$ the level set $\set{x: \cM g(x)>2^k}$. Then (\ref{MgIc}) implies that \begin{equation} \Omega_k\subset 2B \quad \textrm{when}\quad 2^k \ge \frac{C\, \norm{g}{1}\,}{ \mod{B}}. \end{equation} Let $\Omega_k=\bigcup_i Q^k_i$ be a Whitney decomposition of $ \Omega_k$ into closed cubes $Q^k_i, \; i \in \BN$, whose interiors are disjoint, and whose diameters are comparable to $\delta$ times their distances from $\Omega_k^c$, where $\delta$ is a (small) positive constant to be chosen later. Define $\tilde{Q}_i^k$ as the cube with the same centre as $Q_i^k$ and side length expanded by a factor $2$. Then $\bigcup_i\tilde{Q}^k_i= \Omega_k$ and the family $\set{\tilde{Q}^k_i: i\in \BN}$ will have the bounded overlap property, uniformly in $k$, provided that $\delta$ is small enough. Proceeding as in the proof of the atomic decomposition for $H^1(\lambda)$ in \cite[p. 107--109]{St2}, one shows that there exists a decomposition \begin{equation} g=\sum_{k,i} A^k_i, \end{equation} with the following properties. \begin{itemize} \item[\rmi] Each function $A^k_i$ is supported in a ball $B^k_i$ that contains the cube $\tilde{Q}^k_i$ as well as those $\tilde{Q}^{k+1}_m$ that intersect $\tilde{Q}^k_i$. Moreover, if $\delta$ is sufficiently small, the ball $B^k_i$ is contained in $\Omega_k$ and for each $k$ the family $\set{B^k_i}_i$ has the bounded overlap property. \item[] \item[\rmii] $A^k_i=\lambda_{k,i} \,a^k_i$, where $a^k_i$ is a Lebesgue atom associated to the ball $B^k_i$ and $$\sum_{k,i} \mod{\lambda_{k,i}}\le C\, \norm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. $$ \item[] \item[\rmiii] $\mod{A^k_i}\le C\,2^k$ for each $k$ and $i$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $\Omega_k=\{\cM g>2^k\}$, decompose it into Whitney cubes and quote the resulting decomposition $g=\sum A^k_i$ with properties (i)-(iii).

nodes.name: Split the decomposition at $2B$ and conclude
nodes.statement:
We split the sum in (ef{ad}) in two parts  egin{align*} g&=\sum_{B^k_i
ot\subset 2B}A^k_i\ +\sum_{B^k_i\subset 2B} A^k_i =\Sigma_1+\Sigma_2. \end{align*} Clearly, $\Sigma_2$ is an atomic decomposition with atoms associated to balls contained in $2B$. Thus, it suffices to show that $ \Sigma_1$ is a multiple of an atom associated to $2B$. And indeed, $\Sigma_1$ is supported in $2B $ and has integral zero, because it is the difference of $g$ and $ \Sigma_2$, both of which have these two properties. Moreover, by mi\ and miii\ $$ \mod{\sum_i A^k_i}\le C\,2^k. $$ Hence by (ef{hi}) $$ \mod{\Sigma_1}\le\sum_{ 2^k \,<\,C\,
orm{g}{1}/\mod{B}}\mod {\sum_i A^k_i}\le  rac{C\,
orm{g}{1}}{\mod{B}}\le  rac{C}{\mod {2B}}\,
orm{g}{H^1(\lambda)}. $$ Thus $\Sigma_1$ is a multiple of an atom associated to $2B$. We thus have the desired atomic decomposition of $g$, and the norm estimate (ef{ne}) also follows.
nodes.statement_short: Show the part with balls leaving $2B$ is a single multiple of an atom on $2B$, giving the decomposition and the norm estimate.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion
nodes.statement: In this proof, the constants $C$ may depend on $r$ and $n$. Since any Gaussian $(1,\infty)$-atom is also a Gaussian $(1,r)$-atom, $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ is a subspace of $H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ and $\norm{f}{H^{1,r}(\gamma)}\le\norm{f}{H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $(1,\infty)$-atom is a $(1,r)$-atom, so $H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)\subset H^{1,r}(\gamma)$ with norm inequality.

nodes.name: Transfer a Gaussian $(1,r)$-atom to a Lebesgue atom
nodes.statement: Conversely, suppose that $a$ is a Gaussian $(1,r)$-atom associated to the ball $B \in \mathcal{B}_1$. Then the function $a\,\gamma_0$ is a multiple of a Lebesgue $(1,r)$-atom. Indeed, $\int a\gamma_0\wrt\lambda=\int a\wrt\gamma=0$ and, by the equivalence of the Gauss and Lebesgue measures on admissible balls, $$ \norm{a\gamma_0}{L^r(\lambda)}\le C\,\lambda(B)^{1/r-1}. $$ Hence, $a_0\gamma$ is in $H^1(\lambda)$ with norm at most $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Show $a\gamma_0$ is a multiple of a Lebesgue $(1,r)$-atom, hence lies in $H^1(\lambda)$ with norm $O(1)$.

nodes.name: Apply the decomposition lemma
nodes.statement: By Lemma \ref{cptsupp}, it has a decomposition $$ a\,\gamma_0=\sum_j\lambda_j \alpha_j, $$ where each $\alpha_j$ is a Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atom associated to a ball $B_j$ contained in $2B$. Moreover $$ \sum_j\mod{\lambda_j}\le C, $$ and each $B_j$ is admissible at scale $2$.
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $a\gamma_0$ into Lebesgue $(1,\infty)$-atoms on balls inside $2B$, admissible at scale $2$.

nodes.name: Pull back to Gaussian $(1,\infty)$-atoms and conclude
nodes.statement: Define $a_j=\alpha_j\,\gamma_0^{-1}$. Then $\int a_j\wrt\gamma=0$, and by the equivalence of the Gauss and Lebesgue measures on $B_j$ \begin{align*} \norm{a_j}{\infty}\le C \gamma(B_j)^{-1}. \end{align*} Thus the $a_j$ are multiples of Gaussian $(1,\infty)$-atoms. Since $a=\sum_j\lambda_j a_j$, we conclude that $a \in H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)$ and \begin{equation} \norm{a}{H^{1,\infty}(\gamma)}\le\,C \sum_j\mod{\lambda_j}\le C. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Divide by $\gamma_0$ to obtain Gaussian $(1,\infty)$-atoms and sum the coefficients.

nodes.name: Set up the intersecting-balls inequality
nodes.statement: Let $x \in \supp \mlo f$. We write $\rho = |x|$ and $c = |c_B|,$ so that $B \subset B(c_B, \min(1,1/c))$. The balls $B$ and $B(x, \min(1,1/\rho))$ must intersect, and so \begin{equation} |x-c_B| \le \min(1,1/c) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For $x\in\supp\mlo f$ the balls $B$ and $B(x,\min(1,1/\rho))$ meet, bounding $|x-c_B|$.

nodes.name: Reduce to a scale comparison
nodes.statement: To prove the lemma, it is enough to show that \begin{equation} \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3 \min(1,1/c), \end{equation} since it then follows that $x \in B'$.
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove $\min(1,1/\rho)\le 3\min(1,1/c)$.

nodes.name: Case analysis on $c$
nodes.statement: Now $c - \rho \le |x-c_B|$, so that (\ref{eq:dist}) implies \[ c - \min(1,1/c) \le \rho + \min(1,1/\rho). \] Considering the cases $c \le 1$ and $c > 1$, we conclude from this that \begin{equation} \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Treat $c\le 1$ and $c>1$ to obtain the symmetric inequality (\ref{eq:le}).

nodes.name: Use monotonicity of $t\mapsto t^{-1}-t$ and conclude
nodes.statement: The function $t \mapsto t^{-1} - t, \;\; t>0$, and its inverse are clearly decreasing. Considering the values of this function at $t = \min(1,1/c)$ and $\min(1,1/\rho)/3$, we see that (\ref{eq:3}) is equivalent to \[ \max(1,c) - \min(1,1/c) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho). \] Because of (\ref{eq:le}), this inequality follows if \[ \max(1,\rho) + \min(1,1/\rho) \le 3\max(1,\rho) - \frac13 \min(1,1/\rho) \] or equivalently $\frac43 \min(1,1/\rho) \le 2\max(1,\rho),$ which is trivially true. We have proved (\ref{eq:3}) and the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Convert the target into an inequality implied by (\ref{eq:le}) and check it trivially.

nodes.name: Reduce to a single Gaussian atom
nodes.statement: We shall prove that for any Gaussian atom $a$ \begin{equation} \norm{\mlo a}{1}\le C, \end{equation} from which the lemma follows. \par
nodes.statement_short: It suffices to prove $\|\mlo a\|_1\le C$ for every Gaussian atom $a$.

nodes.name: Dispose of the exceptional atom and localise the support
nodes.statement: Since (\ref{MaEa}) is obvious if $a$ is the constant function $1$, we assume that $a$ is associated to an admissible ball $B$. By the preceding lemma, $\supp \mlo f$ is contained in the ball denoted $B'$. \par
nodes.statement_short: The constant atom is trivial; for the others the support of $\mlo a$ sits in $B'$ by the support lemma.

nodes.name: Bound the first term of the splitting of $\phi_t*a$
nodes.statement: The integral of $\mlo a$ over $2B$ with respect to $\ga$ is no larger than $C$, since $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a \le C \sup |a| \le C/\gamma(B)$. To estimate $\mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a$ at a point $x$ in the remaining set $B'\setminus 2B$, we take $\phi \in \Phi$ and $0 < t < \min(1,1/\mod{x})$ and estimate $a*\phi_t(x)$. We can assume that $t > d(x, B)$ so that $t > |x-c_B|/2$, since otherwise $\phi_t*a(x)$ will vanish. Write \begin{equation} \phi_t*a(x) = t^{-n} \int \left(\phi\big(\frac{x-y}t\big) -\phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big)\right)\,a(y) \wrt y + t^{-n} \phi\big( \frac{x-c_B}t\big) \int a(y) \wrt y. \end{equation} Here the first term to the right can be estimated in a standard way by $$ C t^{-n-1} \int_B |y-c_B| \, |a(y)| \wrt y \le C\ |x-c_B|^{-n-1}\ r_B\ \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Estimate $\int_{2B}\mlo a\,d\gamma$ trivially and split $\phi_t*a(x)$, bounding the cancellation term in the standard way.

nodes.name: Bound the Lebesgue integral of the atom
nodes.statement: To deal with the second term, we estimate $\int a(y)\wrt y$, knowing that the integral of $a$ against $\ga$ vanishes. Thus $$ \int a(y)\wrt y = \int a(y) \frac{\ga_0(c_B) - \ga_0(y)}{\ga_0(c_B)}\wrt y. $$ The fraction appearing here is \begin{equation} e^{|c_B|^2}\left(e^{-|c_B|^2} - e^{-|y|^2}\right) = 1 - e^{(c_B-y)\cdot(c_B+y)}, \end{equation} and the last exponent stays bounded for $y \in B$. Thus the modulus of the right-hand side of (\ref{eq:fraction}) is at most $C|c_B-y| |c_B+y| \le C r_B (1+|c_B|).$ Since $\int |a|\,d\ga \le 1$, this implies \[ |\int a(y)\wrt y| \le C r_B (1+|c_B|) \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}. \] For the last term in (\ref{eq:max}), we thus get the bound $C |x-c_B|^{-n} r_B (1+|c_B|) \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the vanishing Gaussian integral and boundedness of the exponent to bound $\int a\,dy$, hence the second term.

nodes.name: Integrate the pointwise bound over $B'\setminus 2B$
nodes.statement: Putting things together, we conclude that for $x \in B'\setminus 2B$ $$ \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a(x) \le C |x-c_B|^{-n-1} r_B \ga_0(c_B)^{-1} + C |x-c_B|^{-n} r_B (1+|c_B|) \ga_0(c_B)^{-1}. $$ An integration with respect to $\wrt \ga$, or equivalently $\ga_0 \wrt \lambda$, then leads to $$ \int_{B'\setminus 2B} \mathcal{M}_{\mathrm{loc}}a(x)\wrt \ga(x) \le C + C r_B (1+|c_B|) \log\frac{\min(1,1/|c_B|)}{r_B} \le C, $$ and (\ref{MaEa}) is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Combine both bounds and integrate to obtain $\|\mlo a\|_1\le C$.

nodes.name: Necessity of both conditions
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f\in\huat{\gamma}$. Then $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ by Lemma \ref{necn}. To prove the necessity of the condition $E(f)<\infty$, it suffices to show that $E(a)<C$ for all Gaussian atoms $a$. This is obvious for the exceptional atom $1$. If $a$ is associated to a ball $B \in \cB_1$, it follows from the inequality $$ \mod{\int_{-\infty}^{-x} a\wrt\gamma}+\mod{\int_{x}^{\infty} a\wrt \gamma}\le \ \1_B(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ from Lemma \ref{necn}, and $E(a)<C$ for every atom gives $E(f)<\infty$.

nodes.name: Set up the converse construction
nodes.statement: Conversely, assume that $f$ is a function in $L^1(\gamma)$ such that $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E(f)<\infty$. We shall prove that $f\in H^1(\gamma)$, by constructing a Gaussian atomic decomposition $f= \sum_j\lambda_j\,a_j$ such that $\sum_j \mod{\lambda_j}\le C \big (\norm{\mlo f}{1}+E(f)\big)$. \par Most of the following argument, up to the decomposition (\ref{aat}), works also in the $n$-dimensional setting. Since we shall need it in the next section, we carry out that part in $\BR^n$.\par
nodes.statement_short: Announce the construction of a Gaussian atomic decomposition, valid in $\BR^n$ up to (\ref{aat}).

nodes.name: Normalise so that $\int f\,d\gamma=0$
nodes.statement: By subtracting a multiple of the exceptional atom $1$, we may without loss of generality assume that \begin{equation} \int f\wrt\gamma=0. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Subtract a multiple of the exceptional atom to assume vanishing total integral.

nodes.name: Covering by maximal admissible balls and partition of unity
nodes.statement: Let $\set{B_j}$ be a covering of $\BR^n$ by maximal admissible balls. We can choose this covering in such way that the family $\set{\frac12 B_j}$ is disjoint and $\set{4 B_j}$ has bounded overlap \cite[Lemma 2.4]{GMST1}. Fix a smooth nonnegative partition of unity $\set{\eta_j}$ in $\BR^n$ such that $\supp \eta_j \subset B_j$ and $\eta_j=1$ on $\tfrac{1}{2}B_j$ and verifying $ \mod{\nabla\eta_j}\le C/r_{B_j}$. Thus $f=\sum_j f \eta_j$. We now need the following lemma. \par
nodes.statement_short: Choose a bounded-overlap covering $\{B_j\}$ and a smooth partition of unity $\{\eta_j\}$ subordinate to it.

nodes.name: Define the constants $b_j$ and apply the localisation lemma
nodes.statement: Continuing the proof of Theorem \ref{char}, we define $b_j\in\BC$ for each $j \in \BN$ by \begin{equation} \int_{-\infty}^\infty (f-b_j)\eta_j \wrt \gamma =0. \end{equation} Note that since $\eta_j=1$ on $\frac12 B_j$, \begin{equation} \mod{b_j} = \left|\frac{\int{f\eta_j}\wrt\gamma} {\int \eta_j \wrt \ga}\right|\le C \frac{1}{\gamma(B_j)}{\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma}. \end{equation} We now apply Lemma \ref{Lemma1} with $g=f - b_j$ and use the subadditivity of $\mlo$ combined with (\ref{1st}), to get \begin{align} \int \mlo\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)\wrt\lambda&\le\,C\, \int_{4B_j} \mlo f \, \gamma_0(c_{B_j})\wrt\lambda \,+\,C\, \frac {\ga(4B_j)}{\ga(B_j)}\int_{B_j} \mod{f}\wrt \gamma \nonumber \\ &\le\,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma. \end{align} \par
nodes.statement_short: Fix $b_j$ by the vanishing-mean condition, bound $|b_j|$, and derive the local estimate (\ref{3d}).

nodes.name: Atomise each localised piece
nodes.statement: We can now finish the proof of Theorem \ref{char}. By Lemmata \ref{Lemma2} and \ref{cptsupp}, each function $(f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0$ has an atomic decomposition $ \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \alpha_{jk}$ where the $\alpha_{jk}$ are Lebesgue atoms with supports in $2B_j$ and $$ \sum_k \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le \,C\, \int_{4B_j} \mlo f \wrt\gamma. $$ As we saw in the proof of Theorem \ref{1infty}, each $a_{jk}=\gamma_0^{-1} \alpha_{jk}$ is a multiple of a Gaussian atom, with a factor which is independent of $j$ and $k$. Thus \begin{align} f=\sum_j (f-b_j)\eta_j +\sum_j b_j \eta_j = \sum_j \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \,a_{jk} +\sum_j b_j \eta_j. \end{align} and $$ \sum_{j,k} \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le \sum_j \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma \le \,C\, \norm{\mlo f}{L^1(\gamma)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma \ref{Lemma2} and Lemma \ref{cptsupp} to obtain Gaussian atoms and the decomposition (\ref{aat}).

nodes.name: One-dimensional decomposition of $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$
nodes.statement: To complete the proof of Theorem \ref{char}, we need to find an atomic decomposition of $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$. It is here that we must restrict ourselves to the one-dimensional case and that the global condition $E(f) <\infty$ plays a role. \par Choose the intervals $I_0=(-1,1)$, $I_j=(\sqrt{j-1}, \sqrt{j+1})$ for $j\ge 1$ and $I_j=-I_{\mod{j}}$ for $j\le -1$. The intervals $I_j$ have essentially the same properties as the balls $B_j$ introduced above, and we can use them instead of the $B_j$ to construct $\eta_j$ and $b_j$ as before. To decompose now $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$, we first normalise the functions $\eta_j$, letting \[ \tilde{\eta}_j = \frac{\eta_j}{\int \eta_j \wrt \ga}. \] Then $b_j\eta_j = \int f \eta_j \wrt \ga \; \tilde{\eta}_j$, and clearly \[ \sum_{j\ge k}\int f \eta_j \wrt \ga = \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga, \quad k \in \BZ, \] where $\mu_k(x) = \sum_{j\ge k} \eta_j(x).$ Notice that $\int f \mu_k \wrt \ga \to 0$ as $k \to \pm \infty$, in view of (\ref{int0}). A summation by parts now yields \begin{equation} \sum_{j\in \BZ} \int f \eta_j \wrt \ga \; \tilde{\eta}_j = \sum_{k\in \BZ} \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga \; (\tilde{\eta}_k - \tilde{\eta}_{k-1}). \end{equation} But $\tilde{\eta}_k - \tilde{\eta}_{k-1}$ is $C$ times a Gaussian atom, if we use admissible balls at some scale $s>1$ in the definition of atoms. Thus (\ref{eq:**}) is our desired atomic decomposition of $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$, provided we can estimate the coefficients by showing that \begin{equation} \sum_{k\in \BZ}\left| \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga \right| \le\,C\,\left(\norm{f}{1}+ E(f)\right). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Replace balls by the intervals $I_j$, normalise the $\eta_j$ and use summation by parts to write $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$ in atoms.

nodes.name: Estimate the coefficients by $E(f)$ and conclude
nodes.statement: To this end, observe that $$ \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga =\int f(x)\int_{-\infty}^x\mu'_k(y)\wrt\lambda(y)\wrt\gamma(x)=\int \mu'_k(y)\int_y^\infty f(x)\wrt\gamma(x)\wrt\lambda(y). $$ Since the support of $\mu'_k$ is contained in $I_k$ and $$ \mod{\mu_k'(y)}\,\le\, \frac{C}{\mod{I_k}}\,\le\, C \,\big(1+\mod{c_{I_k}} \big), $$ we obtain, using also the bounded overlap of the $I_j$, \begin{align*} \sum_{k\in \BZ}\left| \int f \mu_k \wrt \ga \right| &\,\le\,C \sum_k\int_{I_k}\big(1+\mod{c_{I_k}}\big)\ \mod{\int_y^\infty f(x)\wrt\gamma(x)}\wrt\lambda(y) \\ &\le C\int_{-\infty}^\infty (1+\mod{y}) \mod{\int_y^\infty f\wrt \ga}\wrt \lambda(y) \\ &= C\int_{0}^\infty (1+y) \left(\mod{\int_y^\infty f\wrt \ga}+\mod{\int_{-y} ^\infty f\wrt \ga}\right)\wrt\lambda(y) \\ &\le\, C\big(\norm{f}{1}+ \,E(f)\big); \end{align*} here we used (\ref{int0}). This concludes the proof of Theorem \ref{char}.
nodes.statement_short: Integrate by parts against $\mu_k'$ and use bounded overlap to bound $\sum_k|\int f\mu_k\,d\gamma|$ by $\|f\|_1+E(f)$.

nodes.name: Localise the support by the support lemma
nodes.statement: Since the support of $\eta_j$ is contained in $B_j$, the support of $\mlo (g\eta_j\gamma_0)$ is contained in the ball $4B_j$, because of Lemma \ref{supp}.
nodes.statement_short: $\mlo(g\eta_j\gamma_0)$ is supported in $4B_j$.

nodes.name: Rewrite the convolution with a modified bump $\tilde\phi$
nodes.statement: Moreover, for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $x \in 4B_j$ $$ \phi_t*(g\eta_j\gamma_0)(x)=\gamma_0(c_{B_j})\ \tilde{\phi}_t*g(x), $$ where $\tilde{\phi}(z)=\phi(z)\eta_j(x-tz)\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_ {B_j})$. Thus, to prove (\ref{2maxf}) it suffices to show that there exists a constant $C$ such that $\tilde{\phi}\in C\Phi$ for $x\in 4B_j$ and $0<t < \min(1, 1/\mod{x})$.
nodes.statement_short: Factor out $\gamma_0(c_{B_j})$ and reduce the claim to $\tilde\phi\in C\Phi$.

nodes.name: Verify the $C^1$ bounds for $\tilde\phi$
nodes.statement:
The support of $	ilde{\phi}$ is contained in $B(0,1)$ and $$ \mod{	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le  rac{\gamma_0(x-tz)}{\gamma_0(c_{B_j})}\le C, $$ because for $|z| \le 1$  egin{align*} \mod{x-tz-c_{B_j}}\le \mod{x-c_{B_j}}+\mod{tz} \le C\,{\min(1, 1/\mod{c_{B_j}})}. \end{align*} Similarly $\mod{
abla	ilde{\phi}(z)}\le C$, because the gradients $ 
abla_z\eta_j (x-tz)$ and $
abla_z\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_{B_j})$ give the factors $t(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})$ and $t\mod{x-tz}\gamma_0(x-tz)/\gamma_0(c_{B_j})$, respectively, both of which are bounded. This concludes the proof of Lemma ef{Lemma1}.
nodes.statement_short: Check the support, the sup bound and the gradient bound for $\tilde\phi$, finishing the lemma.

nodes.name: Reduce to the large-$t$ part of the grand maximal function
nodes.statement: By the maximal characterisation of the classical space $H^1(\lambda) $, it suffices to show that \begin{equation} \int\cM\left( (f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\right)\wrt\lambda(x)\le \,C\, \int_ {4B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma. \end{equation} Because of (\ref{3d}), all that needs to be verified is that \begin{equation} \int\sup_{\phi\in\Phi}\ \sup_{t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})} \mod{((f-b_j) \eta_j\gamma_0\big)*\phi_t(x)}\wrt\lambda(x) \le \,C\, \int_{4B_j}\mlo f \wrt \gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: By the classical maximal characterisation and (\ref{3d}), only the $t\ge\min(1,1/|x|)$ contribution remains.

nodes.name: Split the integral at $4B_j$
nodes.statement: To prove (\ref{6th}), we split the integral in the left-hand side into the sum $$ \int_{4B_j}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x)+\int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x). $$
nodes.statement_short: Separate the contributions of $4B_j$ and its complement.

nodes.name: Estimate on $4B_j$
nodes.statement: If $x\in 4B_j$, then for $\phi\in\Phi$ and $t\ge\min(1,1/\mod{x})$ \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le t^{-n} \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)-b_j}\wrt \gamma(y)\\ &\le (1+\mod{x})^n\int _{B_j}\big(\mod{f(y)}+\mod{b_j}\big)\wrt\gamma (y) \\ \qquad&\le C\,(1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n\ \,\int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\wrt\gamma(y), \end{align*} the last inequality because of (\ref{1st}). Hence \begin{align*} \int_{4B_j} \cdots \wrt\lambda(x)\, \le \,C\, \ \mod {4B_j}\ (1+\mod{c_{B_j}})^n \int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma \, \le\, C\,\int_{B_j}\mlo f \wrt\gamma . \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Crude bound using $|b_j|\lesssim$ local average of $|f|$, then integrate over $4B_j$.

nodes.name: Estimate on $(4B_j)^c$ and conclude
nodes.statement: If $x\in (4B_j)^c$, we take $\phi$ and $t$ as before and observe that we can assume that $t> d(x, B_j)$, since otherwise the convolution in (\ref{6th}) will vanish. In view of (\ref{mz}) and (\ref{1st}), we then get \begin{align*} \mod{\phi_t*\big((f-b_j)\eta_j\gamma_0\big)(x)}&\le\int _{B_j}\mod {\phi_t(x-y)-\phi_t(x-c_{B_j})}\ \mod{ f(y)-b_j}\,\eta_j(y) \wrt \gamma(y) \\ &\le\,C\, t^{-n-1} \int_{B_j} \mod{y-c_{B_j}}\,\mod{f(y)-b_j}\wrt \gamma (y)\\ &\le \,C\,\frac{1}{d(x,B_j)^{n+1}} r_{B_j}\, \int_{B_j} \mod{f(y)}\wrt\gamma(y). \end{align*} This implies that $$ \int_{(4B_j)^c}\cdots \wrt\lambda(x)\le C\,\int_{B_j}\mod{f}\wrt\gamma\le C\, \int_{B_j} \mlo f \wrt \gamma. $$ We have proved (\ref{6th}) and the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Use cancellation and the smoothness of $\phi_t$ to get a decaying bound, then integrate and conclude.

nodes.name: Construct the chain of maximal admissible balls
nodes.statement: We shall construct atoms whose supports form a chain connecting $B(0,1)$ to $B$. First we define a finite sequence of maximal admissible balls \[ \tilde{B} _0 = B(0,1),\, \tilde{B}_1, \ldots, \tilde{B}_{N }, \] all with centres $c_{\tilde{B}_{j}}$ on the segment $[0, c_B]$. The absolute values $\rho_j= |c_{\tilde{B}_{j}}|$ shall be increasing in $j$, and the boundary $\partial \tilde{B}_j$ shall contain $c_{\tilde{B}_{j-1}}$ for $j = 1,\ldots,N-1$, which means that \begin{align} \rho_{j} - \frac{1}{\rho_{j}}=\rho_{j-1}, \qquad j=1, \ldots,N-1, \end{align} and $\rho_{0} = 0, \; \;\rho_{1} = 1$. Finally, $N$ is defined so that $\tilde{B}_{N-1}$ is the first ball of the sequence that contains $c_B$, and $\tilde{B}_{N } = B.$
nodes.statement_short: Build $\tilde B_0=B(0,1),\ldots,\tilde B_N=B$ with centres on $[0,c_B]$ satisfying the recursion $\rho_j-1/\rho_j=\rho_{j-1}$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Bound the chain length $N$
nodes.statement: Squaring (\ref{recursive}), we get $$ \rho_{j}^2-\rho_{j-1}^2=2 - \frac1{\rho_{j}^2}\ge1, $$ so that $\rho_{N-1}^2 \ge N-1$. It follows that \begin{equation} N \le |c_B|^2 + 1. \end{equation} \par
nodes.statement_short: Squaring the recursion gives $\rho_{N-1}^2\ge N-1$, hence $N\le |c_B|^2+1$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Define the intermediate bumps and the telescoping pieces $g_j$
nodes.statement: Next, we denote by $B _j, \;\;j=1,\ldots, N$, the largest ball contained in $\tilde{B}_j \cap\tilde{B}_{j-1} $. Notice that the three balls $\tilde{B}_j, \tilde{B}_{j-1}$ and $B _j$ have comparable radii and comparable Gaussian measures. Define now functions $\phi _j$ and $g _j$ by setting \begin{align*} \phi _j&=\gamma(B _j )^{-1} \One_{B _j } \quad j=1,\ldots,N, \\ g _j &= \int g \wrt\gamma\, \left(\phi_{j} -\phi _{j-1} \right), \quad j=1,\ldots,N, \\ g_{N+1} &=g -\int g \wrt \gamma \: \phi_{N}. \end{align*} Clearly, \begin{equation} g-\int g\wrt\gamma\: \phi_0 = \sum_{j=1}^{N+1} g _j. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $B_j$, $\phi_j$ and $g_j$ so that $g-\int g\,d\gamma\,\phi_0=\sum_j g_j$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Show each $g_j$ is a multiple of an atom
nodes.statement:
Each function $g _j$ is a multiple of an atom. Indeed, its integral against $\gamma$ vanishes. Moreover, if $1 \le j \le N$, the support of $g _j$ is contained in $	ilde{B} _{j-1}$ and  egin{align*} 
orm{g _j}{\infty}\le (\gamma(B_{j})^{-1} + \gamma(B_{j-1})^{-1}) \int \mod{g}\wrt\gamma\, \le \,C\, \gamma(	ilde{B}_{j-1})^{-1}\ \gamma (B)\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} The support of $\phi_{N+1}$ is contained in $B$ and  egin{align*} 
orm{g_{N+1}}{\infty}\le 
orm{g}{\infty}+\gamma(B)^ {-1}\int \mod{g}\wrt\gamma \le\,C\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} Thus $$ 
orm{g _j}{H^1(\gamma)}\le C\,\gamma(B)\, 
orm{g}{L^\infty}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,N+1. $$
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing integral plus sup-norm bounds give $\|g_j\|_{H^1(\gamma)}\le C\gamma(B)\|g\|_\infty$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Sum the coefficients
nodes.statement:
Summing the coefficients in the atomic decomposition (ef{sumgj}), we then obtain via (ef{balls})  egin{align*} 
orm{g-\int g\wrt\gamma\,\phi_0}{\huat{\gamma}} \,\le\, C\, (N+1) \,\gamma(B) 
orm{g}{L^\infty} \, \le\,C (1+\mod{c_B}^2)\,\gamma(B) \,
orm{g}{L^\infty}. \end{align*} The proof of the lemma is complete.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply the per-atom bound by $N+1$ and use $N\le |c_B|^2+1$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Split off the constant part of $f$
nodes.statement: Let $f$ be a function in $L^1(\gamma)$ such that $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ and $E_+(f)<~\infty$. Write $f=c(f)+f_0$, where $c(f)=\int f\wrt\gamma$. Since $c(f)$ is a multiple of the exceptional atom, it suffices to find an atomic decomposition of $f_0$. Note that $f_0$ satisfies $$ \mlo f_0 \in L^1(\gamma) \qquad\textrm{and}\qquad \int\mod{x}^2\, \mod{f_0(x)}\wrt\gamma(x)<\infty. $$\par
nodes.statement_short: Write $f=c(f)+f_0$ and reduce to decomposing $f_0$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Reuse the decomposition of Theorem \ref{char}
nodes.statement: Let $\set{B_j}$ be the covering of $\BR^n$ by maximal admissible balls and $\set{\eta_j}$ the corresponding partition of unity introduced in the proof of Theorem \ref{char}. As there, we choose numbers $b_j\in\BC$ such that $$ \int_{-\infty}^\infty (f_0-b_j)\eta_j \wrt \gamma =0 \qquad\forall j. $$ Then the argument leading to (\ref{aat}) shows that $$ f_0=\sum_j \sum_k \lambda_{jk} \,a_{jk} +\sum_j b_j \eta_j, $$ where the $a_{jk}$ are Gaussian atoms supported in $4B_j$ and $$ \sum_{j,k} \mod{\lambda_{jk}}\le\,C\, \norm{\mlo f_0}{L^1(\gamma)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Apply the covering, partition of unity and the argument leading to (\ref{aat}) to $f_0$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Reduce to $\sum_j b_j\eta_j$ and record its properties
nodes.statement: It remains only to prove that $\sum_j b_j \eta_j$ is in $\huat {\gamma}$. We write $g_j=b_j \eta_j$ and observe that \begin{equation} \int \sum_j g_j\wrt\gamma=0 \end{equation} because $f_0$ and the $a_{ij}$ have integrals zero. Thus $$ \sum_j g_j=\sum_j\Big(g_j-\int g_j\wrt\gamma \,\phi_0\Big), $$ where $\phi_0$ is as in Lemma \ref{trch}. Since (\ref{1st}) remains valid for $f_0$, we have \begin{equation} \norm{g_j}{\infty}\le C\,\frac{1}{\gamma(B_j)} \int_{B_j}\mod{f_0}\wrt \gamma. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Note the total integral vanishes and bound $\|g_j\|_\infty$ by the local average of $|f_0|$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Apply the chain lemma and sum
nodes.statement: Lemma \ref{trch} thus applies to each $g_j$, and using also the bounded overlap of the $B_j$ we conclude \begin{align*} \norm{\sum_j g_j}{H^1(\gamma)}\,\le \, C\ \sum_j\big(1+\mod{c_{B_j}}^2\big)\ \int_{B_j} \mod{f_0}\wrt\gamma \,\le \, C\,\int \big(1+\mod{x}^2\big)\, \mod{f_0}\wrt\gamma. \end{align*} This concludes the proof of the sufficiency and the norm estimate. \par
nodes.statement_short: Lemma \ref{trch} plus bounded overlap gives the $H^1(\gamma)$ bound by $\int(1+|x|^2)|f_0|\,d\gamma$.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Necessity for nonnegative $f$ by duality
nodes.statement: The necessity of the condition $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ was obtained in Lemma \ref{necn}. To prove the necessity of (\ref{nec}), let $0 \le f \in \huat{\gamma}$. We first observe that the function $x\mapsto \mod{x}^2$ is in $BMO(\ga)$. Indeed, its oscillation on any admissible ball is bounded. Since $BMO(\gamma)$ is a lattice, the functions $g_k(x)=\min\set{\mod{x}^2,k}$ are in $BMO(\gamma)$, uniformly for $k \ge 1$. By the monotone convergence theorem and the duality between $\huat{\gamma}$ and $BMO(\gamma)$, $$ \int \mod{x}^2 f(x)\wrt\gamma(x)=\lim_k \int g_k(x) f(x)\wrt\gamma(x) \le C \norm{f}{\huat{\gamma}}. $$ The theorem is proved.
nodes.statement_short: Use $|x|^2\in BMO(\gamma)$, the lattice property, monotone convergence and $H^1$-$BMO$ duality.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Deduce $f\in H^1(\gamma)$ from the claim
nodes.statement:
We claim that the operator $\mlo$ is bounded on $L^p(\gamma)$ for $1<p\le\infty$. Deferring momentarily the proof of this claim, we complete the proof of the corollary. Suppose that $f$ is in $L^p (\gamma)$. Then $\mlo f$ is in $L^1(\gamma)$, because $$ 
orm{\mlo f}{1}\le

orm{f}{p}<\infty, $$ since $\gamma(\BR^n)=1$. Moreover, $E_+(f)\le

nodes.statement_short: $\mlo f\in L^1(\gamma)$ since $\gamma$ is a probability measure, and $E_+(f)<\infty$ by Holder; apply Theorem \ref{pos}.

nodes.name: Continuity and the dual inclusion
nodes.statement: It also follows that the inclusion $L^p(\gamma)\subset \huat{\gamma}$ is continuous, and by duality we get the continuous inclusion $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$.\par
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of $L^p(\gamma)\subset H^1(\gamma)$ gives $BMO(\gamma)\subset L^{p'}(\gamma)$ by duality.
nodes.section: 4 A characterisation of nonnegative functions in $H^1(\gamma)$

nodes.name: Local $L^p$ bound for $\mlo$
nodes.statement: It remains to prove the claim. We shall use again the covering $\{B_j\}$ from the proof of Theorem \ref{char}. First we observe that the inequality \begin{equation} \norm{\mlo g}{p} \le C\norm{g}{p} \end{equation} holds when $\supp g \subset B_j$, with a constant $C$ independent of $j$. Indeed, $\mlo$ is bounded on $L^p(\la)$, and $\mlo g$ is supported in the ball $4B_j$, where the Gaussian measure is essentially proportional to $d\la$.
nodes.statement_short: For $g$ supported in $B_j$, use $L^p(\lambda)$-boundedness and the local equivalence of measures on $4B_j$.

nodes.name: Sum over the covering
nodes.statement: Given a function $f \in L^p(\ga)$, we write it as a sum $f = \sum f_j$ with $\supp f_j \subset B_j$ and with the sets $\{f_j \ne 0\}$ pairwise disjoint. We can then apply (\ref{eq:Lp}) to each $f_j$ and sum.
nodes.statement_short: Split $f$ into pieces supported in the $B_j$ with disjoint supports and sum the local bounds.
